t: Plan and aim of the session
n: This session is devoted to laboratory work 5. In it we analyse formaldehyde, acetic acid, phenol and acetone in the second distillate, and determine the quantity by the photoelectrocolorimetry (PEC) method. The plan is as follows: we test the second distillate for formaldehyde and acetone, and also for phenol and acetic acid, that is we detect these substances in the distillate. There are two aims: to study the toxicological significance of acetone and formaldehyde in the second distillate and the forensic chemical significance of the identity reactions.

In the session we determine acetone, formaldehyde, phenol and acetic acid in the second distillate. For the work a textbook, the lecture text and study aids are needed. Among the equipment we use a steam distillation apparatus, a funnel, test tubes, reagents and visual materials. The session takes place in a room fitted with special laboratory equipment.

First, distinguish the purpose of the distillates. The first distillate is tested only for HCN, while the second distillate is tested for other substances. The second distillate, 25 ml, is collected in an empty clean flask. It is used for alcohols, aldehydes and ketones, alkyl halides and others. For phenol, cresols, aniline, nitrobenzene and amyl alcohol, NaHCO3 is added to the distillate and it is shaken with ether. Then the ether is evaporated and the concentration is increased in this way.

Let us begin with the toxicological significance of formaldehyde. Formaldehyde is a gaseous substance with a very sharp, suffocating smell. Its 36.5-37.5% aqueous solution is called formalin. Formalin is used as a disinfectant and preservative, and in the chemical industry. A sudden sharp inhalation of a high-concentration solution may cause sudden death. If it enters by mouth, it burns the mucous membrane. Formaldehyde acts on the CNS and causes loss of consciousness and convulsions, and acts on the liver, kidneys, heart and brain. 60-90 ml of formalin leads to death.

Now the properties and use of formaldehyde. Formaldehyde is a gaseous substance with a sharp, suffocating smell; its 36.5-37.5% aqueous solution is called formalin. At low temperature formalin polymerises and is converted into paraformaldehyde, that is paraform, which is poorly soluble in water. Formaldehyde is used as a disinfectant and preservative, in making phenol-formaldehyde resin, in tanning leather and in the synthesis of urotropine. So the properties, the change in the cold and the uses should be remembered separately.

Formaldehyde undergoes metabolism in the body: methyl alcohol and formic acid may be formed as metabolites. We isolate it from the specimen by means of steam, but only a small amount is isolated. The reason is that the aqueous hydrate of formaldehyde, that is methylene glycol CH2(OH)2, distils with difficulty. That is, in aqueous solution formaldehyde is hydrated and is therefore isolated in a small amount. Remember: the low recovery of formaldehyde is connected with hydrate formation.

The first qualitative reaction for formaldehyde is the resorcinol reaction. To 1 ml of the second distillate, 1 ml of a freshly prepared solution of 1% resorcinol in 10% sodium hydroxide is added. The mixture is heated in a boiling water bath for 3-5 minutes. If a violet colour is formed, this indicates formaldehyde. In a second test tube the same reaction is carried out with purified water and the results are compared. That is, the control experiment with water is always performed alongside.

In the codeine reaction, 1-2 drops of distillate are mixed in a porcelain dish with five-times concentrated H2SO4. 1-2 small crystals of the alkaloid codeine are dropped into the mixture. A blue-violet colour is formed at once. So the reaction proceeds quickly, and the immediate appearance of the colour is considered its result.

In the fuchsin-sulphurous acid reaction, 1 ml of distillate is mixed with 2-3 drops of concentrated sulphuric acid. When the mixture has cooled, 1 ml of fuchsin-sulphurous acid solution is added to it gradually. A change of the solution to blue or violet indicates the presence of formaldehyde. The formation of colour is observed for 15 minutes. Adding the reagent gradually and cooling the mixture beforehand are an important part of the procedure.

Let us compare the significance of the qualitative reactions for formaldehyde. The resorcinol reaction has negative significance, because it is also given by many oxidants and by protein breakdown products. Therefore in the resorcinol test, comparison with 1 ml of distilled water in an additional test tube is essential. The reaction of codeine with concentrated sulphuric acid is sensitive and of positive significance. Fuchsin-sulphurous acid gives a blue or violet colour, and quantitative analysis is also based on this. If there is a lot of formaldehyde, the silver mirror and Fehling reactions are also carried out.

The silver mirror and Fehling reactions are based on reduction. For silver oxide, 10% ammonia is added to 5 drops of 1% AgNO3 until the precipitate dissolves. Then 1 ml of distillate is added and the mixture is heated on a water bath. If formaldehyde is present, a silver mirror appears on the walls of the tube or a black precipitate settles. In the Fehling reaction, 2 ml of distillate is mixed with 2 ml of Fehling reagents 1 and 2 and heated over a gas flame for 5-10 minutes. First yellow copper(II) hydroxide, then red copper(I) oxide settles in the precipitate.

The quantity of formaldehyde is determined by the PEC method. Different amounts of formalin are placed in ten test tubes and made up to 5 ml with water, that is a scale is prepared. To each, 1 ml each of 25% sulphuric acid and fuchsin-sulphurous acid is added, and the tubes stand for 30-40 minutes. 5 ml of distillate is placed in the test tube under examination, and no water is added to it. Then the absorbance is measured on the PEC instrument and the quantity is found from the graph.

Now the toxicological significance of phenol. Phenol is widely used in the national economy and the chemical industry, is used with formaldehyde in the synthesis of plastics, and its 3% solution is an antiseptic. Phenol is toxic: on contact with the human body it burns, is rapidly absorbed through the skin and poisons. In poisoning there is severe pain in the digestive tract, then the patient turns pale, turns blue, cardiac activity weakens, convulsions occur and death follows. In the body phenol forms an ester with sulphuric acid and is excreted in the urine. It is oxidised to form hydroquinone and quinhydrone.

t: Phenol poisoning: signs and the corpse
n: Let us look at the signs of phenol poisoning and the changes in the corpse. In poisoning, severe pain in the digestive tract occurs first, then the pain disappears, the patient turns pale and blue, and cardiac activity weakens. In poisoning with a small amount there may be vomiting, diarrhoea, dizziness and blood in the urine; the patient dies in 1-2 days. In the corpse the burnt areas are hard, dry and grey. The stomach is reduced in size, the kidneys are enlarged, and the internal organs smell of phenol.

The physical properties of phenol. Pure phenol is a transparent crystalline substance with a sharp smell. It is poorly soluble in water, well soluble in organic solvents, and also dissolves well in alkali. In the open air it oxidises and takes on a reddish tint. Phenol boils at 181.4 °C and distils with steam. Its 3% solution is used as an antiseptic. These properties are the basis for choosing the method of isolating phenol from the specimen.

Before determining phenols, we isolate them from the distillate with the help of ether. To 10 ml of distillate, 10% NaHCO3 is added to an alkaline medium, then it is shaken 2 times with 5 ml of ether. The ether is passed through a dry filter and divided into three equal parts. Each part is evaporated in a separate porcelain dish, and the reactions are carried out with the residue.

For phenol, the tribromophenol and iron(III) chloride reactions are carried out. In the tribromophenol reaction, the residue in the first dish is dissolved in 1 ml of water and 3-5 drops of saturated bromine water are added. A white precipitate is formed, which dissolves in excess of the reagent. In the FeCl3 reaction, 1-2 drops of freshly prepared FeCl3 solution are dropped onto the residue in the second dish and a blue-violet colour is formed. This colour disappears under the action of water, alcohol, excess reagent and acids.

t: Indophenol reaction and quantity of phenol
n: In the indophenol reaction the residue is mixed with 1 ml of water, and a drop of aniline and 2 ml of chloride of lime are added. The dirty violet colour formed changes to blue under the action of ammonia solution. Remember: the quantity of phenol is determined by gravimetric and volumetric methods.

The quantity of phenol is determined by bromatometry. In general, the quantity of phenol is found by gravimetric and volumetric methods. In the volumetric method, bromine is liberated from a mixture of KBrO3 + KBr + H2SO4. Bromine reacts with phenol to form tribromophenol: C6H5OH + 3Br2 → C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr. Excess bromine reacts with KI to liberate iodine: Br2 + 2KI → I2 + 2KBr. Thus we move on to the calculation stage.

Phenol and cresols must be distinguished. If FeCl3 is added to meta-cresol, a red-violet colour is formed; with para-cresol, a light blue colour. Phenol gives a blue-violet colour with FeCl3. Cresols do not give the indophenol reaction, while phenol gives a dirty violet colour with aniline and chloride of lime. Indophenol is formed on oxidation of a mixture of phenols and amines, including ammonia.

The significance of acetic acid and poisoning with it. Concentrated acetic acid contains 96% CH3COOH, acetic essence 40-80%, and table vinegar 3-8%. When concentrated acid gets on the skin, it burns, causing swelling and ulcers. The lethal amount is 2-15 g, which corresponds to 10-20 ml of acetic essence or 200-300 ml of table vinegar. In the body acetic acid is metabolised to form acetaldehyde, ethyl alcohol and, in part, CO2.

Signs of poisoning with acetic acid. When concentrated acetic acid is drunk, the oesophagus is burnt, and vomiting with blood and diarrhoea occur. Haemolytic anaemia, haemoglobinuria, anuria and uraemia develop. The poisoning runs a milder course than with sulphuric and hydrochloric acid. In the corpse, besides the smell of vinegar, necrosis of the liver and nephrosis of the kidney are found; all this is a guide for forensic chemical examination. The vapours burn the respiratory tract and cause bronchopneumonia and catarrhal bronchitis.

The isolation of acetic acid is based on its volatility. From various specimens it is distilled off with steam; if there is a lot of it, the distillate smells characteristically of vinegar. Distillation makes it possible to determine free acetic acid. For its salts, the specimen is acidified with 10% sulphuric acid to pH 2.5-3.0 and distilled. So that it does not evaporate, the distillate is distilled into a vessel with 0.1 N alkali solution until it is completely isolated. The distillate is made up to an exact volume and divided in two: one part for quantitative analysis, the other dried on a water bath for determination of the acetate ion.

The identity of acetic acid is confirmed by several reactions. In the residue of acetic acid neutralised with FeCl3 a red product is formed, which on heating turns brown; sensitivity 0.5 mg. In the lanthanum nitrate and iodine reaction, if lanthanum nitrate, an alcoholic solution of iodine and ammonia are added to the residue, a dark blue colour or precipitate is formed. In the indigo reaction, if the residue is heated with calcium salts, acetone is formed, from which indigo dye can be made.

We also determine acetic acid by its esters. For ethyl acetate, the residue is heated with ethyl alcohol and concentrated sulphuric acid; an ester with a characteristic smell is formed, sensitivity 5 mg. In the case of amyl acetate, if the residue is heated with amyl alcohol and concentrated H2SO4, the smell of pear essence is perceived. The quantity is determined by the neutralisation method, and the quantity in air by the iodometric method. In iodometry KI and KIO3 liberate iodine in an amount equivalent to the acetic acid, and the iodine is titrated with sodium thiosulphate in the presence of starch.

The quantity of acetic acid in air is determined by the iodometric method. The basis of the method is that KI and KIO3 liberate iodine in an amount equivalent to the acetic acid. The liberated iodine is titrated with a solution of sodium thiosulphate of exact concentration in the presence of starch. The quantity of acetic acid in the solution is determined by the neutralisation method. That is, the amount of iodine is equivalent to the acetic acid.

Acetone, that is dimethyl ketone, is a colourless, transparent liquid with a characteristic smell; it mixes with water and all organic solvents in any proportion. Acetone is included in the list of precursors and is also used in the illicit production of narcotic substances. It belongs to the substances with a narcotic action, accumulates in the body and is eliminated very slowly. Acetone is also formed in a healthy body: in diabetes its content in urine reaches 300-400 mg%, and in the norm 40 mg%. It may also be a metabolite of isopropyl alcohol.

The properties and use of acetone. Acetone is a colourless, transparent liquid with a characteristic smell; it boils at 56.3 °C and is lighter than water. It mixes with water and all organic solvents. If its aqueous solution is saturated with common salt or K2CO3, it separates into two layers. Acetone vapour is heavier than air, so the risk of poisoning is high in enterprises that use it. It is used as a solvent for paints and nitrocellulose, in the synthesis of chloroform, sulfonal and iodoform, and in the production of synthetic rubber and smokeless powder.

The iodoform and nitroprusside reactions for acetone. Acetone forms iodoform with an alkaline solution of iodine; the reaction is sensitive but not characteristic. With sodium nitroprusside, acetone in the presence of alkali forms a red-violet colour; this reaction is also not characteristic. There are interfering substances: ethyl alcohol and lactic acid interfere with the iodoform reaction, and acetaldehyde, methyl ethyl ketone and others with the nitroprusside reaction.

The principle of the iodoform reaction. Acetone, like ethyl alcohol, reacts readily with an alkaline solution of iodine to form iodoform. The reaction is very sensitive but not characteristic of acetone, since ethyl alcohol and lactic acid also give this reaction. As a result yellow iodoform and sodium acetate are formed. An alkaline medium and iodine are the conditions of this process.

The principle of the nitroprusside reaction. Acetone in the presence of alkali forms a red-violet colour with sodium nitroprusside Na2[Fe(CN)5NO]. The reaction is not characteristic of acetone: acetaldehyde, methyl ethyl ketone, acetophenone, acetylacetone and diacetyl also interfere. Therefore furfural, o-nitrobenzaldehyde and GLC are used to confirm acetone.

The furfural and o-nitrobenzaldehyde reactions for acetone. In the furfural reaction, an alcoholic solution of furfural and alkali are added to the distillate, then on adding concentrated HCl a red colour is formed if acetone is present. In the case of o-nitrobenzaldehyde, its saturated solution in 2 N alkali is added; if acetone is present, a blue colour, that is indigo, is formed. If there is little acetone, the reaction proceeds slowly: first yellow, then yellow-green and green-blue colours appear. Indigo dissolves well in chloroform.

Acetone is also determined by the GLC method. For this we use a chromatograph with a flame ionisation detector, and acetone is found by its retention parameters. The quantity of acetone is also determined by GLC. Another feature: if an aqueous solution of acetone is saturated with salts such as common salt, calcium chloride or potassium carbonate, it separates into two layers.

Let us sum up the features of isolation of the substances. Formaldehyde distils with steam only in small amounts, because in aqueous solution it forms a hydrate, that is methylene glycol. So that acetic acid does not evaporate, the distillate is collected in a vessel with 0.1 N alkali, and for its salts the specimen is acidified to pH 2.5-3.0. Acetone distils well with steam. Phenol is isolated with ether after adding NaHCO3.

t: Case: stomach piece with suspected acetic acid
n: The first case concerns a piece of stomach with suspected acetic acid. With the referral, a 200 g piece of stomach from a corpse born in 1950 was brought in a 1-litre plastic container. The inner wall of the stomach has turned very black, the pH of the medium is 2.0-2.5 and it has a specific sharp smell. In the preliminary analysis, when 1 drop of freshly prepared 5% FeCl3 was added to the isolate and heated, a red-brown precipitate formed.

t: Case: phenol (the nurse incident) and case 3
n: This slide gives the nurse incident connected with phenol, and case 3. The nurse used water from a glass container for a cleansing enema. The patient's skin turned blue, the heartbeat slowed, he lost consciousness and died after 2 hours. In the preliminary analysis, the solution from the glass container gave a yellowish-white precipitate with bromine water and a violet solution with iron(III) chloride. In case 3, in pieces of internal organs of a human corpse, the gastric mucous membranes are reduced in size and there is a sharp, suffocating smell. Justify which substances the analysis should be carried out for.

t: Nurse case: the route to finding phenol
n: Let us consider the route to finding phenol in the nurse case. The incident: the nurse used water from a glass container for a cleansing enema, the patient's skin turned blue, the heartbeat slowed, and he died after 2 hours. In the preliminary analysis the solution gave a yellowish-white precipitate with bromine water and a violet solution with FeCl3. Phenol is rapidly absorbed through the skin and poisons, and the tribromophenol and FeCl3 reactions are characteristic of phenol. Therefore the assumption is phenol. Then the solution is made alkaline with NaHCO3, extracted with ether, confirmed by the indophenol reaction and distinguished from cresols, and the quantity is found by PEC or bromatometry.

In the "Wheel" exercise we match reactions to substances. The tribromophenol, indophenol-formation and iron(III) chloride reactions are carried out for phenol. The resorcinol, fuchsin-sulphurous acid, silver oxide and Fehling reactions are carried out for formaldehyde. Exercise: for each substance choose the corresponding reactions and write down the result.

Rules of safety and review questions. The student brings to the laboratory work rubber gloves, a napkin and a face mask. The examination is carried out in rooms with ventilation and a fume cupboard, which are locked and sealed after work is finished. The review questions concern the significance of formaldehyde, its isolation, identity reactions and quantity, the significance of phenol, its isolation, bromine water, FeCl3, indophenol and quantity. Questions are also asked on the significance of acetic acid, its isolation and distillate, and the reactions for establishing the identity of acetone.

Let us conclude. For formaldehyde, the resorcinol reaction gives a violet colour, codeine and H2SO4 blue-violet, fuchsin-sulphurous acid blue or violet; the silver mirror and Fehling reactions are also carried out, and the quantity is determined by PEC. Phenol is isolated with ether; bromine water gives a white precipitate, FeCl3 a blue-violet colour, indophenol a dirty violet, then blue colour. For acetic acid, FeCl3 gives red, then brown, lanthanum nitrate and iodine give dark blue, and esters are also formed. For acetone, iodoform, nitroprusside, furfural, o-nitrobenzaldehyde and GLC are used.
